**Direction:** Adapt active learning selection strategies to prioritize preference pairs where the current reward model is most uncertain about safety-relevant queries. Compare alignment outcomes (safety benchmarks, refusal consistency) when training on actively selected safety-focused pairs vs. random preference selection at matched data budgets.

**Why it matters:** Reducing the human annotation budget for safety-critical alignment while maintaining safety properties would make alignment more accessible for resource-constrained developers.

**Relevant context:** RLTHF targeted human feedback (2025); RLHF efficiency literature; Anthropic HH-RLHF dataset; active learning for NLP.

# Misalignment Localization: Do Emergently Misaligned Models Show Concentrated or Diffuse Representation Changes?

**Problem:** Emergent misalignment produces broad behavioral changes from narrow fine-tuning, but whether these changes correspond to localized representation differences in specific layers or are diffuse throughout the network is unknown. This matters for designing targeted post-hoc corrections.

**Direction:** Apply activation patching and representation analysis (e.g., logit lens, probing classifiers) to compare representations in aligned vs. emergently misaligned model variants at specific layers. Identify whether misalignment-related representations are localized or distributed.

**Why it matters:** If emergent misalignment localizes to specific layers, targeted weight editing or activation steering could reverse it without full retraining — a practically important finding for safety interventions.

**Relevant context:** Emergent misalignment open code; In-Training Defenses (arxiv 2508.06249); mechanistic interpretability literature; representation engineering methods.

Train a probe to distinguish reward-hacking runs from benign runs. Compare probe AUROC against the prompted-monitor AUROC baseline of 0.96 from the MALT paper.

**Why it matters:** If evaluation-awareness probes generalize to reward hacking, this suggests a unified internal representation underlying multiple forms of strategic behavior, with implications for interpretability-based monitoring.

# Monitor False Positive Rate Under Distribution Shift: MALT-Trained Monitors on New Task Families

**Problem:** MALT monitors achieve high AUROC on held-out MALT data, but MALT covers only 30 task families. It is unknown how false positive rates behave when these monitors are applied to task families not represented in training (distribution shift).

**Direction:** Train a simple prompted monitor on the MALT public split. Apply it to a new task family (e.g., creative writing or math reasoning tasks from a public benchmark) where reward hacking is implausible. Measure false positive rate and compare against the 5% FPR reported on the MALT in-distribution test set.

**Why it matters:** High false positive rates on benign task distributions would make MALT-trained monitors impractical for general deployment. This test directly evaluates operational readiness of the best current monitors.

**Relevant context:** MALT monitors at 5% FPR catch 80-90% of true positives in-distribution. The dataset spans software and research tasks; generalization to other domains is untested. Intro-ML students can run prompted monitors via API.

# Comparing Behavioral vs Activation Monitoring Latency for Real-Time Agent Control

**Problem:** Runtime control requires fast detection. Activation probes run in parallel with inference, while behavioral monitors (prompted LLM judges) require an additional inference call. The latency tradeoff between these approaches in a real agentic loop has not been empirically quantified at small scale.

**Direction:** Instrument a simple ControlArena-style agent loop with both an activation probe monitor and a prompted LLM judge monitor on Llama-3-8B. On a set of 50 sandbagging and benign tasks, measure wall-clock latency per step for each monitor type, alongside AUROC. Plot the accuracy-latency Pareto frontier.

**Why it matters:** Practical AI control systems must balance detection accuracy with latency. Quantifying this tradeoff at small scale provides first evidence for whether activation probes are worth the additional engineering complexity over simpler prompted monitors.

**Relevant context:** ControlArena supports custom protocol implementation. Activation probes are described in arxiv 2506.10805. Prompted monitors are evaluated in MALT. Single-GPU setup is sufficient for 7B models.

# Effect of System Prompt Length on CoT Monitorability

**Problem:** CoT monitorability studies typically use standardized or minimal system prompts. Real deployments use long system prompts (tools, personas, context). Whether long system prompts compress or displace safety-relevant reasoning in the CoT is unknown.

**Direction:** Using a fixed set of reward-hacking scenarios from MALT, vary system prompt length (0, 500, 2000, 5000 tokens of benign instructional text) prepended to the prompt. Run a fixed prompted monitor on each and measure AUROC. Report whether monitorability degrades with system prompt length.

**Why it matters:** Enterprise deployments routinely use long system prompts. If monitor accuracy degrades with system prompt length, labs need to account for context window competition when designing monitoring pipelines for real products.

**Relevant context:** CoT monitorability measurement paper (arxiv 2510.23966) defines coverage as key metric. MALT provides standard reward-hacking scenarios. Experiment requires only API calls, making it feasible for CS students.
